opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think exploration is one of the most underrated levers we have, especially now that RL is applied to large language models.

The basic intuition is simple. In reinforcement learning the model only learns from what it actually tries. If the policy never samples a behavior, it never gets a reward signal for it, so it can't learn that the behavior was good. Efficiency in RL isn't only about squeezing more out of each gradient step. It's about whether the data you collect contains anything worth learning from. Exploration is how you make sure it does.

With LLMs there's an interesting twist. Pretraining gives us a very strong prior, so the model already "knows" a huge space of plausible behaviors. In that sense exploration is partly solved for us: we don't need epsilon-greedy over random tokens the way we did in Atari. But that strong prior is also a trap. RL fine-tuning tends to sharpen the distribution. The model collapses onto the few reasoning patterns that worked early, entropy drops, and after a while every rollout for a prompt looks the same. Once that happens, rewards become all-or-nothing across samples, the advantage signal goes to zero, and you're spending compute without learning anything. A lot of what looks like "RL plateaus" or "RL only reweights what the base model could already do" is, I think, really an exploration failure.

So I'd frame it in three layers.

The first is keeping diversity alive during training. Entropy regularization, careful clipping, temperature choices, and not over-optimizing on easy prompts all help the policy keep trying different paths, so the gradient keeps carrying information.

The second is choosing where to explore. Not every problem is equally informative. Problems the model always solves or never solves give you almost no signal. The sweet spot is the frontier, where the model succeeds sometimes. Curriculum design and adaptive sampling of problems are really exploration at the task level, and they can make a big difference in sample efficiency.

The third, and I think the most exciting, is exploration at the level of reasoning strategies rather than tokens. Humans don't explore by randomly perturbing words. We try a different approach, decompose the problem differently, check an intermediate result, or backtrack. If we can get models to explore in that more structured, semantic space, for example by generating diverse plans, revisiting failed attempts, or using their own uncertainty to decide what to try next, then each rollout becomes much more valuable. That's where I think the real gains in efficiency will come from.

Underneath all of this is a broader point: RL can only discover things that are reachable from where the model currently is. Good exploration widens that reachable set, and that determines whether RL just polishes existing abilities or helps the model find genuinely new ones.

r002.rationale: It describes exploration failures and proposes more structured exploration, but does not clearly suggest that current LLMs may lack an active capacity to explore.

r003.rationale: It says to focus exploration on problems where the model sometimes succeeds and that adaptive task sampling can improve sample efficiency, conveying that choosing productive directions reduces the effort needed to make progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that exploration is really the bottleneck for sample efficiency, more than the learning algorithm itself. In most interesting problems, the reward is sparse. If an agent just acts randomly, it almost never stumbles into the behavior you want, so there is nothing to learn from. You can have the most elegant policy gradient in the world, and it will sit there doing nothing because the data coming in carries no signal.

So the question becomes: how do you make the agent go looking for signal on purpose? Early on, people used things like epsilon-greedy, which is basically random noise. That works in small environments but scales terribly, because the chance of randomly chaining together the right sequence of actions drops exponentially with horizon length.

The more interesting approaches try to give the agent an internal reason to explore. Curiosity-based methods reward the agent for visiting states it can't predict well. Count-based or pseudo-count methods reward novelty directly. The intuition is the same: go where you haven't been, because that's where information is. Done well, this turns exploration from a random walk into something more like a directed search over what the agent doesn't yet understand.

But I'd add a caveat that I think gets underappreciated. Exploration is only useful if the agent can actually exploit what it finds. If your representation is bad, you can visit a novel state and not even register that it's novel, or you discover a useful behavior and the policy can't hold onto it. So in practice, efficiency comes from exploration and representation learning working together. Exploration decides what data you collect, and representation decides how much you learn per sample. If either one is weak, you pay for it in environment interactions.

The other thing I'd say is that the problem shifts as you move to large models. With language models and RL, a lot of the exploration now comes from the prior. The model already knows roughly what a reasonable attempt looks like, so you are exploring in a much narrower, more sensible space. That is a huge part of why RL on top of pretrained models has worked so well. The pretrained model is doing the hard part of exploration before RL even starts.

r002.rationale: It says pretrained models make exploration narrower and more sensible; it does not suggest current LLMs may lack an active capacity to explore.

astra-6.text:
I think exploration is fundamentally about deciding which experiences are worth collecting. In reinforcement learning, the agent learns from the consequences of its actions, so its efficiency depends heavily on what it tries. If it keeps repeating familiar actions, it may learn that behavior very well while never discovering a better strategy. But if it explores randomly, it can spend a lot of interactions learning very little.

The goal is to make exploration informative. For example, an agent might try an action because it is uncertain about the outcome and resolving that uncertainty could change its decisions. That’s more useful than seeking novelty for its own sake.

There’s also a time dimension. Sometimes discovering a reward requires a coordinated sequence of actions, so a little random variation at each step won’t get you there. Exploration needs to persist long enough to test a possibility.

So I’d say good exploration makes reinforcement learning more efficient by helping the agent collect experiences that improve its decisions, while balancing that learning against using what it already knows.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss current LLMs or whether they lack an active capacity to explore.

r003.rationale: It says informative exploration can improve decisions and efficiency, but does not explain that choosing a productive direction reduces the amount of research needed to make progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think exploration is really about deciding which experience is worth collecting. In reinforcement learning, an agent learns from its interaction with the environment, so efficiency depends not just on how well it learns from data, but also on how informative that data is.

Random exploration can help, but it can also waste a lot of interactions. More directed exploration tries to identify where the agent is uncertain and where resolving that uncertainty could improve its decisions. There’s a distinction between something you haven’t learned yet and something that is inherently unpredictable—you don’t want the agent to spend all its time chasing randomness.

So the goal isn’t simply to explore more. It’s to balance trying promising actions with gathering information that might reveal better ones. Good exploration can make each interaction more useful, which is especially important when collecting experience is expensive.
